name.text: NEET_UG_BIOLOGY_ANATOMYOFFLOWERINGPLANTS_DIAGRAM_Q01 - Stomatal apparatus with dumb-bell guard cells

questiontext.text: Observe the diagrammatic representation of a stomatal apparatus shown below. Identify the plant group in which this type of stomatal apparatus is characteristically found, along with the correctly matched label for the dumb-bell shaped guard cell.

generalfeedback.text:
Step 1: Given Data and Conditions
The diagram shows a stomatal apparatus in surface view. Label S points to an outer rectangular epidermal cell, label P points to a specialised flanking cell next to the stomatal cell pair, label Q points to one of the two dumb-bell shaped cells with thickened inner walls, and label R points to the central opening between them.

Step 2: Assumptions and Sign Conventions
The schematic represents a standard mature stoma in the leaf epidermis. Cell wall thickness is indicated by line weight, where the inner walls facing the central aperture are noticeably thicker than the outer walls.

Step 3: Relevant Formulae and Principles
In the epidermal tissue system, a stomatal apparatus consists of the stomatal aperture, two guard cells, and surrounding specialised epidermal cells called subsidiary cells. While most plants have bean-shaped guard cells, grasses (monocots) characteristically possess dumb-bell shaped guard cells.

Step 4: Step-by-Step Working
1. Label S indicates the ordinary epidermal cell at the periphery.
2. Label P indicates the specialised subsidiary cell adjacent to the guard cell.
3. Label Q indicates the dumb-bell shaped guard cell, which is a diagnostic feature of grasses.
4. Label R indicates the central stomatal pore enclosed by the two guard cells.

Step 5: Check and Final Answer
Confirming against the anatomy of the epidermal tissue system: dumb-bell shaped guard cells are characteristic of grasses, and label Q points directly to the guard cell. Therefore, the stomatal apparatus belongs to grasses (monocots), and Q represents the guard cell.

answer.text: Dicotyledonous leaves; P represents the guard cell

questiontext.text: Based on the transverse schematic of a single vascular bundle shown below, identify the tissues labelled X, Y, and Z, and the plant organ where this arrangement is characteristically found.

generalfeedback.text:
Step 1: Given Data and Conditions
The schematic shows a single vascular bundle in transverse view. Region X is located on the outer side, region Z is located on the inner side tapering towards the centre, and a narrow meristematic strip Y lies directly between X and Z.

Step 2: Assumptions and Sign Conventions
In standard stem transverse sections, the outer side of the vascular bundle faces the periphery (cortex/epidermis) and the inner tapering end faces the central pith.

Step 3: Relevant Formulae and Principles
In conjoint vascular bundles, xylem and phloem are situated jointly along the same radius, with phloem usually located on the outer side of xylem. When cambium is present between phloem and xylem, the vascular bundle is termed open because it can form secondary xylem and secondary phloem.

Step 4: Step-by-Step Working
1. Since phloem is located on the outer side in a conjoint bundle, X represents phloem.
2. Since xylem is located on the inner side, Z represents xylem.
3. The meristematic band Y situated between phloem and xylem is the cambium.
4. Conjoint, open vascular bundles with cambium are a characteristic feature of dicotyledonous stems (whereas monocotyledonous stems have closed vascular bundles lacking cambium).

Step 5: Check and Final Answer
Verifying all labels and organ association: X is phloem, Y is cambium, Z is xylem, and this conjoint open vascular bundle is characteristically found in a dicotyledonous stem.

answer.text: X = Xylem, Y = Cambium, Z = Phloem; monocotyledonous stem
X = Phloem, Y = Endodermis, Z = Xylem; dicotyledonous root
X = Phloem, Y = Cambium, Z = Xylem; dicotyledonous stem
X = Xylem, Y = Pericycle, Z = Phloem; monocotyledonous leaf

questiontext.text: Observe the schematic transverse section of the root stele and surrounding layers shown below. Based on the number of xylem bundles and the size of the central pith, identify the plant organ and its primary xylem arrangement.

generalfeedback.text:
Step 1: Given Data and Conditions
The schematic transverse section shows a central stele surrounded by pericycle, endodermis, and cortex. Inside the stele, there are 8 distinct radiating xylem arms alternating with phloem regions, and a large, well-developed central pith.

Step 2: Assumptions and Sign Conventions
In the xylem arms, the smaller circles near the periphery represent the narrow protoxylem elements, while the larger circles closer to the centre represent the wider metaxylem elements.

Step 3: Relevant Formulae and Principles
1. In roots, primary xylem is arranged in an exarch manner, meaning protoxylem lies towards the periphery and metaxylem lies towards the centre.
2. Dicotyledonous roots usually have two to four xylem and phloem patches and a small or inconspicuous pith.
3. Monocotyledonous roots usually have more than six (polyarch) xylem bundles and a large, well-developed pith.

Step 4: Step-by-Step Working
1. Counting the radiating xylem bundles in the diagram gives 8 bundles, which is more than six (polyarch condition).
2. The central pith is large and prominent.
3. Both features—polyarch xylem bundles and a large, well-developed pith—uniquely identify the specimen as a monocotyledonous root.
4. Because the narrow protoxylem is positioned towards the periphery and the wider metaxylem towards the centre, the primary xylem arrangement is exarch.

Step 5: Check and Final Answer
Combining the organ identification and xylem arrangement, the diagram represents a monocotyledonous root with exarch primary xylem.

questiontext.text: The diagram below illustrates a lens-shaped opening formed in the periderm of a woody dicotyledonous stem. Identify the structures labelled P, Q, and R, along with the primary function of this opening.

generalfeedback.text:
Step 1: Given Data and Conditions
The transverse section shows a ruptured outer epidermis, a lens-shaped opening filled with loosely arranged rounded cells (P), a narrow rectangular meristematic layer beneath it (Q), and larger rounded parenchymatous cells on the inner side (R).

Step 2: Assumptions and Sign Conventions
The outer surface of the woody stem is at the top of the diagram, and the inner cortical tissues are towards the bottom.

Step 3: Relevant Formulae and Principles
During secondary growth, phellogen (cork cambium) cuts off cork (phellem) on the outer side and secondary cortex (phelloderm) on the inner side. At certain regions, phellogen cuts off closely arranged parenchymatous complementary cells on the outer side instead of cork cells; these rupture the epidermis to form lens-shaped openings called lenticels, which permit gaseous exchange between the outer atmosphere and internal stem tissues.

Step 4: Step-by-Step Working
1. Label P points to the mass of rounded parenchymatous cells rupturing the epidermis, which are the complementary cells.
2. Label Q points to the narrow, rectangular meristematic layer producing these cells, which is the cork cambium (phellogen).
3. Label R points to the parenchymatous layer formed on the inner side of phellogen, which is the secondary cortex (phelloderm).
4. The primary physiological role of a lenticel is gaseous exchange in woody trees.

Step 5: Check and Final Answer
Matching all structures and the function: P represents complementary cells, Q represents cork cambium (phellogen), R represents secondary cortex (phelloderm), and the opening facilitates gaseous exchange.

answer.text: P = Cork cells, Q = Vascular cambium, R = Pith; water conduction
P = Subsidiary cells, Q = Epidermis, R = Mesophyll; transpiration regulation
P = Guard cells, Q = Phelloderm, R = Phellem; translocation of photosynthates
P = Complementary cells, Q = Cork cambium (phellogen), R = Secondary cortex (phelloderm); gaseous exchange
